hops.afterHeading: The problem: one crossing, and only one
hops.title: Why Icelandic horses can move both left legs together
hops.text: Most horses walk, trot and gallop. Many Icelandic horses can also pace, swinging both left legs forward together, then both right legs. In 2012, Lisa Andersson and colleagues linked pacing to a mutation that puts an early stop signal in a gene called DMRT3. Among 352 more Icelandic horses, all but one of the five-gaited ones, which pace, carried two copies; small samples of Thoroughbreds, Arabians and Shetland ponies carried none. In mice the gene is active in spinal interneurons, including some whose axons cross the midline. Mice lacking it have fewer of these crossing neurons, and as newborns their hind legs rarely take turns.

sources.citation: Andersson, L. S. et al. (2012). Mutations in DMRT3 affect locomotion in horses and spinal circuit function in mice. Nature 488:642-646.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A chestnut Icelandic horse crossing a green meadow with both left legs forward together and both right legs back.
image.caption: A DMRT3 mutation helps Icelandic horses pace, moving both left legs together, then both right legs.

hops.afterHeading: Mammals mute Robo, and also clear it
hops.title: When the left half of the brain moved the left side of the body
hops.text: Biology students learn that each half of the brain moves the limbs on the opposite side of the body. That holds because the main motor pathway, the corticospinal tract, crosses in the brainstem during development. In 2015, doctors at Osaka National Hospital described a 55-year-old woman who had lived since childhood with eyes that could not turn sideways and a curving spine. She arrived with sudden weakness on her left side, yet the bleed was in the left half of her brain. Imaging showed her corticospinal tracts had never crossed, and DNA sequencing found two copies of a ROBO3 mutation. After treatment, she improved a great deal and went home.

sources.citation: Yamada, S. et al. (2015). Ipsilateral hemiparesis caused by putaminal hemorrhage in a patient with horizontal gaze palsy with progressive scoliosis: a case report. BMC Neurology 15:25.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Two country lanes running side by side down a green valley, one on each side of a stream, with a footbridge neither lane uses.
image.caption: With a ROBO3 mutation, one woman's main motor pathway never crossed, so her left brain moved her left side.

hops.title: The zebrafish whose fastest escapes went only one way
hops.text: Mice without Robo3 die hours after birth, too soon to test how they walk. In 2009, Harold Burgess, Stephen Johnson and Michael Granato found that a zebrafish mutant called twitch twice had a broken robo3 gene. A larval zebrafish has two giant escape neurons whose axons each cross the midline, so a startling sound can trigger a fast turn to either side within 15 milliseconds. In twitch twice, one of those axons often stays on its own side. Larvae whose two escape axons both ran down the right side turned right in 98.6 percent of their fastest startles. Their slower startles still went either way.

sources.citation: Burgess, H. A., Johnson, S. L. & Granato, M. (2009). Unidirectional startle responses and disrupted left-right co-ordination of motor behaviors in robo3 mutant zebrafish. Genes, Brain and Behavior 8:500-511.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: Overhead view of a tiny translucent zebrafish larva in a dish of clear water, its body curved sharply to one side.
image.caption: When both escape axons end up on the same side, a larva's fastest startle turns go almost entirely that way.
